introduction.p: It is a remarkable fact that algebra, which is about symbolic equations and their solutions, and geometry are intimately connected. For instance, the solution set of a linear equation in two unknowns, such as 2x + y = 1, can be represented graphically by a straight line. The aim of this section is to further this connection by introducing vectors, which will help us to apply geometric intuition to our thinking about linear systems.

subsection.title: Vectors
subsection.p:
vector A vector is most simply thought of as a matrix with a single column. For instance,
\vec{v} = \left[ \begin{array}{r} 2 \\ 1 \\ \end{array} \right]
and
\vec{w} = \left[ \begin{array}{r} -3 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 2 \\ \end{array} \right]
are both vectors. The entries in a vector are called its components. Since the vector \vec{v} has two components, we say that it is a two-dimensional vector; in the same way, the vector \vec{w} is a four-dimensional vector.
We denote the set of all m-dimensional vectors by \real^m. Consequently, if \vec{u} is a 3-dimensional vector, we say that \vec{u} is in \real^3.

While it can be difficult to visualize a four-dimensional vector, we can draw a simple picture describing the two-dimensional vector \vec{v}, as shown in .
A graphical representation of the vector \vec{v} = \twovec21.

We can think of \vec{v} as describing a walk in the plane where we move two units horizontally and one unit vertically. Though we allow ourselves to begin walking from any point in the plane, we will most frequently begin at the origin in which case we arrive at the the point (2,1), as shown in the figure.

There are two simple algebraic operations we often perform on vectors.
Scalar Multiplication scalar multiplication
We multiply a vector \vec{v} by a real number c by multiplying each of the components of \vec{v} by c. For instance,
-3\left[\begin{array}{r} 2 \\ -4 \\ 1 \\ \end{array}\right] = \left[\begin{array}{r} -6 \\ 12 \\ -3 \\ \end{array}\right].
We will frequently refer to real numbers, such as -3 in this example, as scalars to distinguish them from vectors.
Vector Addition vector addition
We add two vectors of the same dimension by adding their components. For instance,
\left[\begin{array}{r} 2 \\ -4 \\ 3 \\ \end{array}\right] + \left[\begin{array}{r} -5 \\ 6 \\ -3 \\ \end{array}\right] = \left[\begin{array}{r} -3 \\ 2 \\ 0 \\ \end{array}\right].

subsection.p: The preview activity demonstrates how we may interpret scalar multiplication and vector addition geometrically.

First, we see that scalar multiplication has the effect of stretching or compressing a vector. Multiplying by a negative scalar changes the direction of the vector. In either case, shows that a scalar multiple of a vector \vec{v} lies on the same line defined by \vec{v}.
Scalar multiples of the vector \vec{v}=\twovec21.

To represent the sum \vec{v} + \vec{w}, we imagine walking from the origin with the appropriate horizontal and vertical changes given by \vec{v}. From there, we continue our walk using the horizontal and vertical changes prescribed by \vec{w}, after which we arrive at the sum \vec{v} + \vec{w}. This is illustrated on the left of where the tail of \vec{w} is placed on the tip of \vec{v}.
Vector addition as a simple walk in the plane is illustrated on the left. The vector sum is represented as the diagonal of a parallelogram on the right.
Alternatively, we may construct the parallelogram with \vec{v} and \vec{w} as two sides. The sum is then the diagonal of the parallelogram, as illustrated on the right of .

We have now seen that the set of vectors having the form c\vec{v} is a line. To form the set of vectors c\vec{v}+\vec{w}, we can begin with the vector \vec{w} and add multiples of \vec{v}. Geometrically, this means that we begin from the tip of \vec{w} and move in a direction parallel to \vec{v}. The effect is to translate the line c\vec{v} by the vector \vec{w}, as shown in .
The set of vectors c\vec{v} + \vec{w} form a line.

At times, it will be useful for us to think of vectors and points interchangeably. That is, we may wish to think of the vector \left[\begin{array}{r} 2 \\ 1 \end{array}\right] as describing the point (2,1) and vice-versa. When we say that the vectors having the form c\vec{v} + \vec{w} form a line, we really mean that the tips of the vectors all lie on the line passing through \vec{w} and parallel to \vec{v}.

observation.p:
Even though these vector operations are new, it is straightforward to check that some familiar properties hold.
Commutativity
\vec{v} + \vec{w} = \vec{w} + \vec{v}.
Distributivity
a(\vec{v} + \vec{w}) = a\vec{v} + a\vec{w}.

subsection.p:
We can perform scalar multiplication and vector addition with {sympy} matrices. We define a vector using sp.Matrix() with either a single row or a single column (our choice will matter!); then * and + denote scalar multiplication and vector addition.
import sympy as sp
v = sp.Matrix([3,1]) w = sp.Matrix([-1,2]) print (2*v) print (v + w)
Note that the vectors v and w defined above are column vectors. That is, v=\twovec{3}{1} and w=\twovec{-1}{2}. In order to define a row vector we can use x = sp.Matrix([[5, -8]]). Notice that we could not compute the sum v + x. Verify this using the Python code cell above and convince yourself why taking such a sum is not permissible.

subsection.title: Linear combinations
subsection.p: Linear combinations, which we encountered in the preview activity, provide the link between vectors and linear systems. In particular, they will help us apply geometric intuition to problems involving linear systems.

Every two-dimensional vector can be written as a linear combination of \vec{v} and \vec{w} because the coefficient matrix of the linear system remains the same. Since that coefficient matrix has a pivot position in every row, the augmented matrix can never have a pivot position in the rightmost column.

subsection.p: This activity illustrates how linear combinations are constructed geometrically: the linear combination c\vec{v} + d\vec{w} is found by walking along \vec{v} a total of c times followed by walking along \vec{w} a total of d times. When one of the weights is held constant while the other varies, the vector moves along a line.

statement.p:
The previous activity also shows that questions about linear combinations lead naturally to linear systems. Suppose we have vectors \vec{v} = \twovec{3}{-1} and \vec{w}=\twovec{4}{3}. Let's determine whether we can describe the vector \vec{b}=\twovec{-11}{-18} as a linear combination of \vec{v} and \vec{w}. In other words, we would like to know whether there are weights c and d such that
c\vec{v} + d\vec{w}= \vec{b}.

To solve this linear system, we construct its corresponding augmented matrix and find its reduced row echelon form,
\left[ \begin{array}{rr|r} 3 \amp 4 \amp -11 \\ -1 \amp 3 \amp -18 \end{array} \right] \sim \left[ \begin{array}{rr|r} 1 \amp 0 \amp 3 \\ 0 \amp 1 \amp -5 \end{array} \right],
giving us the weights c=3 and d=-5; that is,
3\vec{v} -5 \vec{w} = \vec{b} . In fact, we know more because the reduced row echelon matrix tells us that these are the only possible weights. Therefore, \vec{b} may be expressed as a linear combination of \vec{v} and \vec{w} in exactly one way.

subsection.p: This example demonstrates the connection between linear combinations and linear systems. Asking whether a vector \vec{b} is a linear combination of vectors \vec{v_1},\vec{v_2},\ldots,\vec{v_n} is equivalent to asking whether an associated linear system is consistent.

In fact, we may easily describe the associated linear system in terms of the vectors \vec{v}, \vec{w}, and \vec{b}. Notice that the augmented matrix we found in our example was
\left[ \begin{array}{rr|r} 3 \amp 4 \amp -11 \\ -1 \amp 3 \amp -18 \end{array} \right].
The first two columns of this matrix are \vec{v} and \vec{w} and the rightmost column is \vec{b}. As shorthand, we will write this augmented matrix replacing the columns with their vector representation:
\left[ \begin{array}{rr|r} \vec{v} \amp \vec{w} \amp \vec{b} \end{array} \right] . This fact is generally true so we record it in the following proposition.
The next activity puts this proposition to use.

Explain how the pivot positions of the matrix \left[\begin{array}{rrr} \vec{v_1} \amp \vec{v_2} \amp \vec{v_3} \end{array} \right] help answer this question.

We find vectors

No, it is not possible to write every three-dimensional \vec{b} as a linear combination of \vec{v_1}, \vec{v_2}, and \vec{v_3} because the matrix \left[\begin{array}{rrr} \vec{v_1} \amp \vec{v_2} \amp \vec{v_3} \end{array}\right] does not have a pivot position in every row. This means that, with some choice of vector \vec{b}, we will obtain an inconsistent system.

Every vector \vec{b} can be expressed as a linear combination of \vec{v_1}, \vec{v_2}, and \vec{v_3} in exactly one way because \left[\begin{array}{rrr} \vec{v_1} \amp \vec{v_2} \amp \vec{v_3} \end{array}\right] has a pivot position in every row and every column.
The vector \vec{b} cannot be expressed as a linear combination of \vec{v_1}, \vec{v_2}, and \vec{v_3}.

subsection.title: Summary
subsection.p:
This section has introduced vectors, linear combinations, and their connection to linear systems.
There are two operations we can perform with vectors: scalar multiplication and vector addition. Both of these operations have geometric meaning.
Given a set of vectors and a set of scalars we call weights, we can create a linear combination using scalar multiplication and vector addition.
A solution to the linear system whose augmented matrix is
\left[\begin{array}{rrrr|r} \vec{v_1} \amp \vec{v_2} \amp \ldots \amp \vec{v_n} \amp \vec{b} \end{array}\right]
is a set of weights that expresses \vec{b} as a linear combination of \vec{v_1},\vec{v_2},\ldots,\vec{v_n}.
